blindSummary:
For trans visitors this country carries extreme risk, with the most severe documented police practice in its surrounding region. An international human-rights organisation interviewed four transgender women whom the state security agency arrested between 2019 and 2022 solely on the basis of their gender expression in public. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced unlocking of their phones so officers could identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison facility in the capital; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Arrests continued even during a major international sporting event hosted by the country in 2022, under global scrutiny.
blindOutOfScope: Migrant-worker abuse under the sponsorship labour system, and general human-rights concerns, affect all residents; only trans-specific risk to visitors is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation (Oct 2022): documents arbitrary arrest and abuse of LGBT people by this country's security forces, including in preventive detention, ahead of the 2022 international sporting event it hosted.

Encyclopedia overview: same-sex acts illegal since 1938, and religious law may also apply; penalty up to 7 years (a capital penalty is legal but unenforced); no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no relationship recognition; covers the controversy over LGBT treatment at the 2022 sporting event the country hosted, and living conditions.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying legal-aid trust country profile documents this country's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

Regional news site (Feb 2015): police in a regional peer state arrested 23 'cross-dressers and homosexuals' at a chalet party - charged with 'engaging in immoral activities'; homosexual acts between adult men there can draw six years; no LGBT protections - included as context from a co-ordinating sub-regional grouping of states.
Foreign tabloid (April 2019): a survey listing several nations where execution for homosexual acts is lawful - this country appears among those with severe penalties grounded in religious law.

Foreign broadcast network (July 2018): 'Under tournament spotlight, authorities crack down on LGBT news coverage' - a major foreign newspaper's LGBT coverage was censored from the capital's print edition; an official of an international human-rights organisation said the censorship could violate the country's human-rights commitments to the international sports body ahead of the event it hosted in 2022.

LGBT news outlet (July 2018): a foreign prime minister was urged to raise the case of LGBT people in this country during the hereditary ruler's visit to that foreign capital - this country is one of 74 countries punishing same-sex relations with imprisonment; attention focused on its record ahead of the 2022 sporting event.
